q1.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE similarity between fascism and communism as political movements in the twentieth century.
parts.b: Explain ONE difference between fascist and communist ideology, using the historian's interpretation in the passage.
parts.c: Explain ONE cause of the appeal of both fascism and communism in Europe after World War I.

sample_answers.a: Both rejected liberal democracy and individual rights, instead glorifying collective discipline, mass mobilization, and a single party that claimed to embody the will of the people or nation.
sample_answers.b: According to the passage, communists sought to abolish class divisions and private ownership of production, while fascists preserved private property and class hierarchy, demanding instead that all classes submit to the nation and its leader.
sample_answers.c: The war's devastation, economic collapse, and the apparent failure of parliamentary governments to restore order or prosperity discredited liberal democracy and made radical promises of national rebirth or social revolution attractive.

q1.stimulus:
Historians note that fascism and communism, though bitter enemies, shared important features as products of the crisis of liberalism after World War I. Both movements rejected parliamentary democracy as weak and corrupt, celebrated violence and discipline, built single-party states, and used modern propaganda to mobilize entire populations. Yet their visions were fundamentally opposed. Communists, following Marx, sought the abolition of private property and class divisions through international proletarian revolution. Fascists defended private property and social hierarchy but demanded that individuals, classes, and businesses all subordinate themselves to the nation, embodied in an all-powerful leader. Their rivalry was thus not only a power struggle but a contest between two incompatible visions of modernity.
—Historian's account of fascism and communism in the period c. 1900–present

q2.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Identify ONE claim Mussolini makes about the relationship between the individual and the state.
parts.b: Describe ONE way in which fascist ideology differed from communist ideology regarding private property.
parts.c: Explain ONE reason why Mussolini's rejection of socialism appealed to Italian conservatives and business owners.

sample_answers.a: Mussolini claims that the individual exists only within the state, and that fascism demands the subordination of all individual interests to the life and power of the nation-state.
sample_answers.b: Fascism preserved private property and private enterprise (under state direction), while communism called for abolishing private ownership of the means of production and collectivizing industry.
sample_answers.c: Conservatives and employers feared communist revolution and labor unrest; Mussolini promised to crush unions and the left while protecting property, offering order without the threat of expropriation.

q2.stimulus:
Fascism recognizes the real needs which gave rise to socialism and trade unionism, but it rejects the class struggle. For Fascism, the state is absolute: individuals and groups are relative. Fascism is opposed to socialism, which confines the movement of history within the class struggle and ignores the unity of the nation. We demand that the productive forces of the nation — capital and labor — collaborate in the service of the state, rather than destroy each other in conflict.
—Adapted from Benito Mussolini, The Doctrine of Fascism, 1932

q3.directions: Use the image below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE feature of the poster that communicates its political message.
parts.b: Explain ONE way in which the poster reflects communist methods of gaining support after the Russian Revolution.
parts.c: Explain ONE difference between the mass-mobilization techniques shown in the poster and fascist propaganda methods.

sample_answers.a: The sharp red wedge driving into the white circle visually depicts the Bolsheviks (red) piercing and shattering the White armies (white), turning abstract political struggle into a simple, forceful geometric image anyone could understand.
sample_answers.b: The Bolsheviks used bold, modernist art to reach a largely illiterate population, presenting the civil war as a clear struggle between revolution and counterrevolution and calling ordinary people to identify with the red cause.
sample_answers.c: Communist art like this emphasized collective struggle and abstract ideological forces, while fascist propaganda typically centered on the glorified figure of the leader and on emotional appeals to national humiliation and rebirth.

q3.stimulus: The image is El Lissitzky's 1919 poster Beat the Whites with the Red Wedge, created during the Russian Civil War. A sharp red triangle (symbolizing the Bolshevik Red Army) drives into a white circle (symbolizing the anti-Bolshevik White forces). The poster is a landmark of revolutionary avant-garde art, using abstract geometric shapes to deliver a political message to a largely illiterate population.
